analysis.one_liner: Ends tax deferral on overseas corporate profits and closes foreign tax loopholes.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee hearing or a vote; it was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it stayed until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change how U.S. corporations are taxed on money their foreign subsidiaries earn. Today, that money generally goes untaxed until it is brought back to the United States. The bill would tax it every year instead, take away a foreign tax credit from the largest oil companies, tighten rules on that credit overall, and require foreign corporations that are actually run from the United States to pay U.S. taxes like domestic ones. It was introduced by Sen. Bernie Sanders and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, in the form of added federal revenue from corporations that currently pay little or no U.S. tax on profits booked overseas. Domestic companies that compete against multinationals with foreign profit-shifting would also face fairer ground.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would eliminate deferral, meaning U.S. corporations would owe U.S. tax on their foreign subsidiaries' profits each year instead of only when the money is repatriated [S2, S3].

It would deny the foreign tax credit to large integrated oil companies that are dual capacity taxpayers—firms that pay foreign governments in exchange for economic benefits—closing a channel used by the largest oil companies [S2, S3].
It would limit the foreign tax credit so it only offsets income actually subject to U.S. tax, by restoring a per-country credit limit [S2, S3].

It would treat foreign corporations that are managed and controlled primarily in the United States as domestic corporations for tax purposes, including publicly traded companies and firms with $50 million or more in assets [S2, S3].

analysis.who_pays: Multinational U.S. corporations with foreign subsidiaries, the largest integrated oil companies, and investment firms that operate from the United States but are chartered abroad. Some costs could be passed to consumers and shareholders.
analysis.who_pays_short: Multinationals, big oil, offshore investment firms

drawbacks.text: Critics of ending deferral argue it would raise the tax burden on U.S.-based multinationals relative to foreign competitors and could encourage companies to redomicile abroad, though the bill would counter that by taxing U.S.-managed foreign corporations as domestic [S2, S3].

The bill took aim at some of the most powerful lobbies in Washington—the oil industry and major multinationals—and carried no bipartisan co-sponsorship beyond one Democratic senator, which critics would say showed it had no realistic path [S4, S5].
Ending deferral is a major change to international tax rules; businesses would face significant compliance costs and restructuring during the transition [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would raise significant federal revenue from corporations that legally avoid U.S. tax on foreign profits, with the main cost falling on the multinationals and oil companies targeted. The serious counterargument is the risk that U.S. companies lose ground to foreign rivals or move their legal homes abroad; the bill tries to block that route but enforcement would depend on regulations Treasury had not yet written. It was never debated, so no committee-amended version exists to weigh.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on February 7, 2013 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never held a markup or vote, and it died there when the Congress ended in January 2015 [S1, S5].

narrative.text: Sen. Sanders introduced the Corporate Tax Dodging Prevention Act on February 7, 2013 [S1, S5].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance on the day it was introduced; no further action was ever taken [S5].
The bill attracted only one cosponsor, a Democratic senator, during its two years in the chamber [S4].
The Finance Committee never reported the bill, and the full Senate never considered it before the 113th Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Multinational corporations and large oil companies kept the ability to defer U.S. tax on foreign profits and to claim foreign tax credits, at no cost, because the bill never advanced. U.S. taxpayers saw no change in the tax gap it targeted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Multinationals and oil companies kept existing tax rules

for.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill, introduced it in the Senate on February 7, 2013.

for.name: A Democratic Senate cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, its only second supporter in the chamber.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair: Sen. Max Baucus)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on February 7, 2013 and never held a markup, hearing, or vote on it; the bill died at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; an independent senator sponsored the bill with a single Democratic cosponsor and no Republican support appeared in the record [S4].

industries.note: The bill would end their ability to defer U.S. tax on foreign subsidiary profits, meaning annual U.S. tax on income currently deferred indefinitely. Keeping the status quo preserves a revenue gap ordinary taxpayers effectively cover.

The bill would deny them the foreign tax credit for payments to foreign governments that buy them special economic benefits, a provision written to hit companies with over $1 billion in gross receipts and at least 500,000 barrels of daily production. Losing that credit would raise their U.S. tax bill.

industries.industry: Investment management and funds managed from the U.S.
industries.note: Foreign-chartered firms whose decisions about investor assets are made in the United States, or whose executive officers are primarily U.S.-based, would be taxed as domestic corporations. That would close a structure used by offshore investment vehicles.
